common_name: Flamingo Chinese Toon (Pink Spring Shoot Toona)

planting.note: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun.

directions: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun. Keep the root zone evenly moist while the tree establishes, and prune hard each late winter to keep the plant at a manageable shrubby size that resprouts with an even heavier flush of the prized pink shoots. The blush-colored young leaves and shoot tips share the same onion-garlic, slightly resinous flavor as the green-leaved species and are harvested the same way, stir-fried or folded into egg dishes while still tender. Because the pink coloring is most vivid in filtered light, 'Flamingo' doubles as a striking foliage accent for a partly shaded edible garden bed.

planting.note: Establish Daruma wasabi by planting healthy rhizome divisions or crowns in spring into cool, constantly moist, richly organic soil kept below about 70F, ideally alongside a shaded stream bank or in a heavily mulched bog bed fed by clean, moving water.

directions: Establish Daruma wasabi by planting healthy rhizome divisions or crowns in spring into cool, constantly moist, richly organic soil kept below about 70F, ideally alongside a shaded stream bank or in a heavily mulched bog bed fed by clean, moving water. Daruma is the cultivar most commonly grown by commercial wasabi farms in North America because of its vigorous growth and comparatively good tolerance of temperature swings, though it still demands full to partial shade and unfailing moisture to avoid rot or stunting. After 18 to 24 months the thick rhizome is ready to harvest and grate fresh, releasing the same clean, sinus-clearing heat that fades within minutes, a world apart from the horseradish-and-dye paste sold as wasabi in most restaurants. Its dense, heart-shaped leaves also make an attractive textural groundcover for a deeply shaded, moisture-rich corner of the garden.

common_name: Alexandria Alpine Strawberry (Heavy-Bearing Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start Alexandria's dust-fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since germination depends on light exposure and steady moisture at room temperature, then transplant the young clumps into rich, well-drained soil after the last frost.

directions: Start Alexandria's dust-fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since germination depends on light exposure and steady moisture at room temperature, then transplant the young clumps into rich, well-drained soil after the last frost. It performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, making it one of the more shade-adaptable strawberries for tucking beneath taller vegetables, shrubs, or fruit trees where full-sun beds are unavailable. Alexandria is valued among seed-grown alpine strawberries for its unusually heavy, extended production of small, intensely sweet, aromatic red berries with true wild-strawberry perfume. Because the runnerless plants stay in a tidy clump, they also work well as a low edible edging along a partly shaded path or border.

common_name: Brussels Winter Chervil (Cold-Hardy Heirloom Anise Herb)

planting.note: Direct-sow Brussels Winter chervil seed shallowly into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in late summer or early fall, since this old cold-hardy strain thrives on a fall-to-spring schedule and resents the heat that makes most chervil bolt.

directions: Direct-sow Brussels Winter chervil seed shallowly into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in late summer or early fall, since this old cold-hardy strain thrives on a fall-to-spring schedule and resents the heat that makes most chervil bolt. Give it a partly shaded spot with dappled light, where its fern-like foliage stays tender and productive right through cold snaps that would finish off less hardy sowings. The leaves carry chervil's signature mild anise-parsley flavor, best used fresh and added at the end of cooking to season eggs, soups, and delicate sauces. Because it holds quality in cold, shaded conditions better than standard chervil, Brussels Winter is a reliable way to keep a fresh culinary herb coming from a shady bed through the off-season.

common_name: Wentworth American Highbush Cranberry (Early-Ripening Fruit Selection)

planting.note: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Wentworth shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil, choosing a site with a half-day of shade if the location has hot afternoon sun.

directions: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Wentworth shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil, choosing a site with a half-day of shade if the location has hot afternoon sun, since this selection tolerates woodland-edge conditions better than many fruiting shrubs. Wentworth was selected for producing earlier-ripening, larger, better-flavored clusters of tart red berries than typical seedling highbush cranberries, though a second unrelated seedling nearby improves pollination and fruit set. The berries soften and mellow after a frost and cook down into a bright, tart preserve or sauce reminiscent of true cranberry, a useful substitute in regions where cranberry bogs are not practical. Its tolerance of part shade and reliable fruit set make Wentworth a good choice for a hedgerow or forest-garden edge planting where full sun is not available all day.

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant them into consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants generously since 'Giganteus' is the larger-leaved, more dramatic form of Japanese butterbur commonly offered by nurseries.

directions: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant them into consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants generously since 'Giganteus' is the larger-leaved, more dramatic form of Japanese butterbur commonly offered by nurseries. Its rounded leaves can exceed three feet across on stout petioles, creating a bold, almost tropical look in a shaded, damp corner of the garden where few other food plants would thrive. The thick petioles are harvested in early spring before the leaves fully unfurl and prepared the traditional Japanese way, peeled, blanched, and simmered in dashi or miso as fuki. Because the rhizomes spread aggressively in wet shade, confine 'Giganteus' with a buried barrier or dedicate it to a naturally moist, shaded low spot where its size and vigor become an asset rather than a nuisance.

common_name: Rosina Sweet Violet (Long-Blooming Pink Fragrant Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions of Rosina in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where it spreads slowly by short stolons into a fragrant, well-mannered groundcover.

directions: Plant divisions of Rosina in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where it spreads slowly by short stolons into a fragrant, well-mannered groundcover. Unlike the deep-purple species type, Rosina bears soft pink, sweetly perfumed flowers over an unusually long season from late winter into spring, with a light repeat in fall in mild climates. Both the flowers and young leaves are edible, the blossoms often crystallized in sugar, tossed into salads, or steeped into a fragrant syrup, with a mild, faintly sweet flavor and the same honeyed violet scent. Its shade tolerance, extended bloom, and edible flowers make Rosina a useful choice for a woodland edge or shaded cottage bed where color and food value are both wanted.

common_name: September Sun Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Variegated Fruiting Kolomikta Kiwi)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting of September Sun in spring against a sturdy trellis or fence in humus-rich, well-drained soil, and pair it with a male Actinidia kolomikta vine nearby since this cultivar is a fruiting female that needs a pollinator to set fruit.

directions: Plant a rooted cutting of September Sun in spring against a sturdy trellis or fence in humus-rich, well-drained soil, and pair it with a male Actinidia kolomikta vine nearby since this cultivar is a fruiting female that needs a pollinator to set fruit. Give it a site with dappled or filtered light rather than harsh all-day sun, which keeps the foliage's dramatic pink-and-white variegation from scorching while the vine still ripens its small, smooth-skinned, sweet kiwiberries in late summer. The grape-sized fruit tastes like a sweeter, thinner-skinned version of grocery-store kiwifruit and can be eaten skin-and-all straight off the vine. Because it thrives with part-shade protection and doubles as an ornamental accent, September Sun suits a partly shaded arbor or fence where both fruit and foliage color are wanted.

common_name: Ben Nevis Black Currant (Heavy-Cropping Scottish Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root Ben Nevis bushes in early spring, several inches deeper than they grew in the nursery row to encourage a multi-stemmed base, into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in part shade to full sun.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root Ben Nevis bushes in early spring, several inches deeper than they grew in the nursery row to encourage a multi-stemmed base, into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in part shade to full sun. This Scottish-bred cultivar is prized on commercial currant farms for its heavy, reliable yields of large, glossy black berries that ripen a little later than older Ben-series varieties, which helps spread out the harvest window. The berries carry black currant's intense, tart, aromatic flavor and high vitamin C content, and are traditionally cooked into jams, cordials, and the French liqueur cassis rather than eaten fresh off the bush. Like other currants, Ben Nevis fruits well with several hours of daily shade, making it one of the more shade-tolerant fruiting shrubs for a partly wooded garden edge.

common_name: Jolico Cornelian Cherry (Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown Jolico in early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade, giving it room to grow into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown Jolico in early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade, giving it room to grow into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Jolico is an Austrian selection prized for its unusually large, pear-shaped, bright red fruit, up to twice the size of the wild species, produced on a plant that still tolerates the dappled light of a woodland edge better than most fruiting shrubs. The tart-sweet, cranberry-like fruit ripens in late summer and is traditionally cooked into jams, syrups, and sauces, though fully ripe fruit can also be eaten fresh. A part-shade planting slows ripening slightly but the shrub remains healthy and productive, making Jolico a good fit for the partly shaded fringe of an edible landscape.
